item.title: MS NOW Reporter Barred From White House After Trump Imposes Press Ban
item.description:
MS NOW said on Saturday that two of its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds, a day after President Trump announced a ban on three news organizations because of reporting he disliked.

Akayla Gardner, a White House correspondent for MS NOW, said that her White House-issued access badge failed to work at the security entrance where reporters typically enter near the West Wing.

“The officer asked me to hand over my badge; he said that it was disabled,” Ms. Gardner said in an on-air interview. “I asked why I could not get inside; he said it was above him.”

A photographer for MS NOW was also asked to relinquish their badge, but a producer for the network was allowed into the White House, Ms. Gardner said.

MS NOW said in a statement that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

Mr. Trump abruptly announced on Friday afternoon that he would ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House, a stark escalation in his ever-expanding battles with the news media.

The president attributed the ban to his displeasure with the outlets’ coverage of his administration. “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday afternoon.

“Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house,” the president added.

The White House press office declined to answer questions on Saturday about Ms. Gardner’s experience, referring instead to Mr. Trump’s comments on Friday.

Any such prohibition would almost certainly face a legal challenge, and CNN and Politico on Friday suggested that they would fight a ban in court. In Mr. Trump’s first term, the White House lost a similar legal battle after it revoked the press pass for the CNN reporter Jim Acosta, whose credentials were later restored.

Journalists from CNN and MS NOW had been working at the White House as usual on Friday evening. It was unclear if journalists from those outlets had yet attempted to enter the White House on Saturday morning.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs and Benjamin Mullin contributed reporting.

item.title: With Boats Getting Bigger, Money Is Flowing Into Marinas
item.description:
Tanned and tousled after a sailing regatta on Narragansett Bay, more than a thousand people gathered last month at a large marina in Newport, R.I., for three days of competitive racing, dockside dinners and drinks aboard superyachts.

Events like these bring together people who, naturally, love boats. Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard, which hosted the gathering, turned its marina into an entertainment destination for the spectators and potential year-round customers.

As the rich get richer, their boats are also getting bigger and more expensive. And all of those vessels need places to dock and get repairs.

The private equity firm Blackstone sees opportunity in the booming boat business. In the past two years, the company has been on a buying spree of scarce waterfront infrastructure. Its infrastructure fund went from owning zero marinas in 2024 to roughly 200 marinas today — more than anyone in the world.

The company paid $5.6 billion in early 2025 for Safe Harbor, which at the time owned and operated 138 marinas in the United States and Puerto Rico, including dozens of marinas from Maryland to Maine as well as the Caribbean’s largest in Fajardo, P.R. It also runs nine marinas on the Mediterranean, catering to large yachts in places like St. Tropez, Antibes and Monaco.

In November, Blackstone bought the largest marina in Annapolis, Md., and a Maine shipyard on upper Penobscot Bay. Last month, it announced plans to buy 65 marinas and storage facilities from MarineMax for $1.5 billion. The deal is expected to close by the end of this year.

In recent years, Blackstone has snapped up businesses known for their recurring cash flow, in industries like HVAC services and rental housing. Heidi Boyd, senior managing director for Blackstone Infrastructure, said the marinas were a natural fit for its infrastructure fund.

“A lot of what we do is buying businesses that have been around for a long time, and have a natural scarcity to them, like an airport, like a port, like a marina,” she said.

As Safe Harbor adds marinas, it is emphasizing its membership model. Boaters who rent a slip at one of its marinas are considered members, eligible for free stays at any of the other marinas in its network.

But having a corporation like Blackstone buy often independently-run marinas, potentially upgrading and expanding them to bring more billionaire yacht owners to the area has made some boaters and local residents uneasy.

Some residents have written letters to city and county officials asking how they plan to deal with potential noise disturbances, increased traffic and electricity demands, and safe fuel storage for megayachts.

When Safe Harbor announced plans this year to expand operations at a smaller marina in Wareham, Mass., it faced pushback from some residents.

James Morrissey retired to Wareham in 2019 after vacationing and sailing in the area for decades. He said the marina, which abuts his property, was encroaching deeper and deeper into the residential neighborhood, especially with its recent proposal for a 42,000-square-foot building.

“We thought it was way too big, way too large-scale, and it would change the character of the neighborhood,” Mr. Morrissey said while sitting on his porch as a sea breeze moderated a sultry afternoon last month. “It would be like me standing in the backyard and looking at the Fenway Green Monster.”

Safe Harbor has since withdrawn its application for the project, said Christine Santos, a conservation agent for Wareham, “but the Wareham residents still have questions, comments and concerns if, or when, they may come in front of us again.”

In response to the criticism, a Blackstone spokesperson said that Wareham was “an attractive location with lots of customer interest, but we prioritize working with the local community we serve and listening to all potential concerns.”

In Rockland, Maine, Kyle Swan, who has worked as a boat captain and commercial diver, is concerned that the marina Safe Harbor bought there in 2020 could outgrow its corner of the harbor.

“I’m worried about the traffic, and the busyness of Safe Harbor, and the needs of the people who have these big megayachts,” Mr. Swan said. “There’s a load of money in this business now, and the small guy is getting shifted out.”

It seems to him, these days, that “it’s all the big yachts and the big money that’s really cooking,” he said.

Blackstone is not alone in its quest to amass a portfolio of marinas. InfraVia Capital Partners, a private equity firm, bought a group of 28 marinas in nine countries from Spain to the United Arab Emirates, which have 1,000 superyacht berths among its 14,300 total. Bain Capital is also in the marina game through a partnership with BlueWater Marinas.

Andrew Cantor, who represents owners selling marinas at the commercial real estate services company Colliers, said that marina consolidation began to gather steam about a decade ago. He said a boat-buying boom during the Covid-19 pandemic made marinas more valuable, accelerating the trend.

Jason Spalding, a marina adviser, broker and consultant at International Marina Services, said he thought Blackstone would keep acquiring marinas “to continue to feed the machine.”

“I’d be surprised if there was any full-service marina greater than 200 slips that hasn’t been approached by Safe Harbor or some of these larger entities over the past five years,” he said.

A decade ago, there were perhaps four main buying groups among the marina clusters, Mr. Spalding said. He is now tracking 42 buying groups in the United States and Canada, including 14 that own or manage a dozen marinas or more.

“You are going to see continued interest by the private equity groups, continued interest by the infrastructure funds, continued consolidation,” Mr. Spalding said. “There’s so much demand, and such limited supply.”

item.title: Mistakes? We’ve Made a Few
item.description:
For most of its existence, The New York Times corrected errors of spelling and facts with a sentence or two, usually tucked inside the newspaper. It wasn’t until it was well into its second century that the paper began to dig deeper into its own lapses and explain its mistakes to readers, or at least some of them. Corrections moved to more prominent positions, typically Page 2 or the front of the second section, and sometimes even to the front page.

One of the first signs of this new era came in the early 1980s, when Abe Rosenthal, the executive editor at the time, created the “editors’ note,” designed, he said in a memo announcing the new policy, to “amplify articles or rectify what the editors consider significant lapses of fairness, balance or perspective.” Rosenthal wrote one of the first notes himself in 1985 after he objected to what he said was the snide tone of a Times story about a friend, Mortimer Zuckerman, the publisher and real estate developer. “Through opinionated phrases and unattributed characterizations, the article established a tone that cast its subject in an unfavorable light,” said the note, which was unsigned.

“A Correction: Times Was in Error on North’s Secret-Fund Testimony.,” published on July 13, 1987. Read the article or see the original print page.

By 1987, under a different executive editor, Max Frankel, The Times published a correction of more than 1,200 words — as long as many news stories — addressing mistakes in an article that recounted the congressional testimony of Lt. Col. Oliver L. North about the Iran-contra scandal. This appeared on July 13, 1987, under a headline that ran across two columns of the front page: “A Correction: Times Was in Error on North’s Secret-Fund Testimony.”

The remedy may have seemed excessive. “I wouldn’t have insisted on putting a correction on the top of Page 1 to make a point,” Joseph Lelyveld, whom Frankel later named his managing editor, told me years later for a book I wrote on the modern history of The Times.

But the world was changing. This was the post-Watergate and the post-Vietnam War era. There was more skepticism and scrutiny of big institutions, including The Times. Critics and readers were finding new platforms to challenge what The Times was reporting, even before the explosion of social media. The paper, which had long enjoyed an if-it’s-in-The-Times-it-must-be-true status, was under pressure to account for missteps and, at times, the failings of its reporters and editors. In short, to acknowledge that the paper itself, like the institutions it covered, was not immune to errors.

Over the years, this direction of travel has remained constant, producing shifts in the way The Times responds to potential errors and criticism from readers. In 2003, more than 15 years after Rosenthal wrote that editors’ note, The Times appointed Allan M. Siegal, an assistant managing editor who had long served in an informal role as the paper’s internal watchdog, as its first standards editor, and created the position of public editor. The appointments came after The Times discovered that a young reporter had systematically fabricated and plagiarized stories that had appeared in its pages.

The Iraq war was another factor. The Times’ coverage of the lead-up to the conflict promoted the idea that Saddam Hussein was on the verge of assembling a stockpile of weapons of mass destruction. After re-examining its reporting, the newspaper conceded that it had been too credulous in its work, and strengthened its procedures around its use of unnamed sources.

The public editor position was eliminated in 2017. But in 2020, as the newsroom expanded in size and onto new platforms, The Times created a team of seven editors, working under the standards editor, to become the newsroom’s voice for all standards and ethics questions relating to content and news coverage. More recently, The Times formed a Trust team to explain the paper’s decision-making to readers and help field and grapple with complaints.

For all this, it can still take a while to fix an error, with results appearing only after weeks of prodding (and re-reporting). The small still has the tendency to triumph over the large. The paper might, for instance, correct a reporter’s mistaken reference to Tweetie Pie (Tweety Bird!), but leave unaddressed deeper and more consequential errors of judgment. The Times all but ignored the Holocaust, a failure Max Frankel explored in an article written for The Times’ 150th anniversary. It also largely brushed aside concerns that its Moscow correspondent in the 1930s, Walter Duranty, downplayed the existence of the genocidal famine in Soviet Ukraine caused by Stalin’s policies.

However flawed it may sometimes be in its execution, the ethic of addressing errors has continued to drive the newspaper. Here’s (an admittedly incomplete) look at a few of the more notable mistakes The Times has corrected over the years.

“The Times and Wen Ho Lee,” published on September 26, 2000. Read the article or see the original print page.

In March 1999, The Times wrote the first in a series of stories, columns and editorials that portrayed Wen Ho Lee, a Taiwanese-born American scientist assigned to the Los Alamos National Laboratory, as a spy who helped China steal nuclear secrets to build bombs. Lee was indicted by a federal grand jury in New Mexico on 59 counts related to illegally moving classified information from the Los Alamos weapons lab to an easily accessible computer. He was branded a security risk, was imprisoned without bail and spent nine months in solitary confinement. But the case ended when Lee pleaded guilty to a single count of mishandling classified information.

In a note from the editors titled “The Times and Wen Ho Lee,” published on Sept. 26, 2000, The Times said it stood by much of the story, but acknowledged the criticism that “contended that our reporting had stimulated a political frenzy amounting to a witch hunt.”

“We could have pushed harder to uncover weaknesses in the F.B.I. case against Dr. Lee,” the note said. “In place of a tone of journalistic detachment from our sources, we occasionally used language that adopted the sense of alarm that was contained in official reports and was being voiced to us by investigators, members of Congress and administration officials with knowledge of the case.”

The note did not announce any changes in editorial procedures at the paper but instead said it had instructed its reporters to go back and continue their reporting. “Our coverage of this case is not over,” it said.

“Times Reporter Who Resigned Leaves Long Trail of Deception,” published on May 11, 2003. Read the article or

In one of the most significant breakdowns in Times history, Jayson Blair, a young reporter at the paper, wrote articles that contained both plagiarized information from other news outlets and outright fabrications. As Blair later acknowledged, he had made up stories in his apartment while telling editors he was on the road. He resigned in 2003 after questioning by editors. “The Times apologizes to its readers for a grave breach of its journalistic standards,” the executive editor, Howell Raines, said in a story about the reporter’s deceptions. Less than two weeks later, a team of Times reporters produced an exhaustive accounting of Blair’s work that appeared on the front page, under the headline: “Correcting the Record; Times Reporter Who Resigned Leaves Long Trail of Deception.”

Raines and his managing editor, Gerald Boyd, did not participate in the preparation of the story. Raines was at his weekend home in Pennsylvania when he saw the Sunday front page. He immediately thought that his career at The Times was over, he told me years later. He was correct; both he and Boyd left the paper.

“The Times and Iraq,” published on May 26, 2004. Read the article or

After the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, The Times ran stories by Judith Miller, a national security reporter, and others based largely on anonymous sources suggesting that the United States had evidence that Iraq was gathering materials to build weapons of mass destruction. These accounts contained warnings about the threat a nuclear-armed Iraq posed to the United States and world security.

On May 26, 2004, after sustained criticism, and with a new public editor about to publish a column, the newspaper issued an editors’ note, nearly 1,200 words long, titled “The Times and Iraq.” The stories, it said, were too often dependent on Iraqi exiles and defectors whose credibility had been challenged at home.

“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” the note said. “In some cases, information that was controversial then, and seems questionable now, was insufficiently qualified or allowed to stand unchallenged. Looking back, we wish we had been more aggressive in re-examining the claims as new evidence emerged — or failed to emerge.”

“A Riveting ISIS Story, Told in a Times Podcast, Falls Apart,” published on December 18, 2020. Read the article or

In 2018, The Times released “Caliphate,” a 12-part podcast series focused on an Islamic terrorist network. Many of the episodes were based on the story of a man calling himself Abu Huzayfah, who said he was a member of the Islamic State and had taken part in killings in Syria. More than two years later, Mr. Huzayfah was arrested by the Canadian police and charged with perpetrating a terrorist hoax. The police said he had even fabricated his identity: His real name was Shehroze Chaudhry.

The Times published an editors’ note saying that, after the arrest, it had re-examined Mr. Chaudhry’s account and “found a history of misrepresentations by Mr. Chaudhry and no corroboration that he committed the atrocities he described in the ‘Caliphate’ podcast.”

“As a result, The Times has concluded that the episodes of ‘Caliphate’ that presented Mr. Chaudhry’s claims did not meet our standards for accuracy,” the note went on. “It is also clear that elements of the original fact-checking process were not sufficiently rigorous,” it added. “Times journalists were too credulous about the verification steps that were undertaken and dismissive of the lack of corroboration of essential aspects of Mr. Chaudhry’s account.”

The Times returned a Peabody Award it had received for the coverage. It affixed an editors’ note to the web page for each “Caliphate” podcast episode and added a new installment to the series, “An Examination of ‘Caliphate,’” which discusses the missteps. The newspaper also assigned an editor to create a process to vet stories produced by the audio unit.

Of course, not all corrections rise to this level of significance. Which is not to say they can’t still be mortifying. The name of the family that owns The Times can be challenging to spell. That said, one would think The Times, of all news organizations, would get the boss’s name down. Nope. “An article in Business Day on Wednesday about investors in The New York Times Company who withheld their votes for directors misspelled the name of the family that has controlled the company since 1896. It is Ochs-Sulzberger, not Ochs-Sulzburger.”

This was hardly the only eyebrow-raising institutional mistake. The newspaper of March 14, 1995, celebrated the 50,000th issue of The New York Times. A correction followed: There had been a miscount, and the milestone would not come for another year.

And, if you’re wondering, some mistakes never happened. Yes, The Times has a strict policy on honorifics. But no, Meat Loaf, the musician, was never referred to as “Mr. Loaf” on second reference. Believable, to be sure, but incorrect.

item.title: Out of Work, and Too Young for Medicare? Here’s What to Consider.
item.description:
What can a laid-off worker over 50 do to get health insurance?

Besides staying healthy until Medicare kicks in at age 65, the answer is: Not a lot.

“Finding affordable health insurance is a huge challenge for people 50 and older,” said Alan Weil, senior vice president of public policy for AARP. “There may be options, but most of them are not very good.”

About 60 percent of people younger than 65 get their health insurance through employers, according to the health-care policy research foundation KFF. But the coverage disappears when workers are laid off. While many replace their insurance when they land a new job, older workers, on average, remain unemployed for much longer than younger ones, with some never earning a new paycheck.

Among workers employed for at least three years who lost their jobs from 2023 through 2025, 72.9 percent of those under 55 found jobs by January 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The rate of re-employment for those 55 to 64, however, was 57.3 percent. While just 9 percent of the younger workers who lost jobs during those years left the work force entirely, 21 percent of those 55 and older never returned.

Besides losing their health insurance, laid-off workers take a financial hit that makes it a hardship to pay for the few health care options available to the unemployed. “Among long-tenured displaced workers who returned to full-time wage and salary employment, only about half were earning as much or more than they had in the job they lost,” Deepali Vyas, head of data at the talent advisory firm ZRG Partners, said in an email.

If you do lose your job, check with your human resources department to find out if your workplace coverage ends on your last day or continues until the end of the month, said Stephanie Heathman, chief executive of the HR Innovator Group. “Employees should never assume that a final paycheck deduction means their health coverage continues through the end of the month,” Ms. Heathman said. “The plan’s eligibility terms determine when active coverage ends.”

If you’re married to someone who can add you to their workplace coverage, moving to their group policy may be your best option. Job loss is a “qualifying event” that allows your spouse to add you to his or her coverage outside of their employer’s annual open enrollment period. This option may also be available for a domestic partner, depending on the employer’s policies. But act fast — federal law gives you just a 30-day window.

Older unemployed workers can — and do — find coverage to tide them over until they qualify for Medicare, but they’ll need to compare all the options, watch out for onerous limits and abide by some strict deadlines.

Here’s a look at what is available.

Losing a job also gives you 60 days to sign up for Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare, coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace at HealthCare.gov. This has been one of the top options until this year, when Congress ended the Biden administration’s five years of enhanced federal subsidies for those with annual household income of more than 400 percent of the federal poverty level. The subsidies now stop at household income of $63,840 for a single person in the 48 contiguous states and Washington, D.C., and $132,000 for a family of four. Ten states offer their own additional subsidies and one, New Mexico, fully offsets the federal cuts, according to healthInsurance.org, a consumer guide affiliated with insurance agencies. Virginia and Rhode Island have approved a limited subsidy for 2027.

Your A.C.A. subsidy is calculated on your total household income for the current year, including your earnings to date, severance pay and any other income.

Before moving to a marketplace policy, note that all of your co-payments and out-of-pocket costs for the year will reset with your new policy. If you’ve already met those limits under your former employer’s policy, it may be less expensive to continue that coverage under COBRA for the rest of the year, then enroll through the marketplace for 2027.

Under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985, workers who have their hours reduced or lose their jobs for any reason other than gross misconduct can opt to stay on their employer’s health care plan. COBRA benefits generally last for 18 months. The catch is that you’ll now pay both your share of the premium and your employer’s share, plus an administrative fee of up to 2 percent. For many people, that can be more than double what had been deducted from their paycheck.

One COBRA hack is that you’ve got 60 days to sign up. This gives you a bit of time to land another job, find other coverage or briefly wait to see if you develop an injury or illness that would make COBRA a good choice. If you sign up, you’ll still need to pay premiums for the entire 60-day period. Check with your former employer’s H.R. department about the deadline, which can vary. If you miss it, you’re unlikely to get the coverage.

One way to cut that cost is to move qualified dependents to other health insurance options. For example:

If a spouse qualifies for Medicare, your job loss is a qualifying event that gives them eight months to enroll in Medicare.

Whether or not they were enrolled in your workplace plan, a spouse or dependent who was eligible under your plan has a 30-day special enrollment period to switch to their employer’s plan. Dependent children up to age 26 also have 30 days to enroll in their own workplace plan or another parent’s plan.

Spouses and children who were enrolled in the former employer’s plan can enroll in COBRA (and pay the premiums) even if the fired worker does not. They have the same 60-day window to apply.

A growing number of doctors offer basic primary care in exchange for a monthly cash retainer, using a subscription model. The monthly costs can range from as little as $60 to as much as $250, depending on where you live, said Dr. Harsha Moole, a hospitalist based in Topeka, Kansas, who’s a partner in FindMyDirectDoctor.com, a referral service for cash-pay physicians.

Dr. Moole said he grew frustrated admitting patients to the hospital because they lacked a doctor who could provide preventive care. “Then their blood pressure got out of control, gave them a stroke or heart attack, and I’m admitting them into the hospital for reasons that could have been prevented by a $10 pill,” Dr. Moole said.

Doctors offering direct primary care work with compounding pharmacies and medical labs to offer discount or wholesale-priced medications, services and tests to their patients. Dr. Moole also advised buying a high-deductible insurance policy to cover catastrophic care. This model has been compared to car insurance — auto owners pay to maintain their vehicles but retain insurance for large, expensive accidents. Some plans available at HealthCare.gov, like bronze or, for certain applicants, catastrophic coverage, have high deductibles but provide all the Affordable Care Act protections.

Before signing up with a direct primary care doctor, review your last several years of medical care with the physician, along with projected future needs, such as colonoscopies, vision care and treatments for diabetes or other chronic conditions, plus tests and specialist care, such as OB-GYN treatment. Shopping for a high-deductible insurance policy will also require checking the fine print to see whether your particular conditions are excluded and to identify any limits or caps on treatment.

These limited policies, sold by private insurers, usually have low premiums and can be used as a bridge until you find other coverage. Under federal law, new policies are restricted to three months, and a total of four months with any renewal. But since August 2025, the Trump administration has said it won’t enforce those limits and is creating new rules for these policies. In any event, you should check the rules of your state, since it may maintain its own limits.

You’ll need to shop very carefully for these policies, which are exempt from Affordable Care Act requirements, meaning they can deny coverage for pre-existing conditions and don’t have to cover essential benefits, such as mental health or maternity care. The policies can have strict dollar limits and coverage caps, and set prices based on age, health status, gender and other factors.

“Truthfully, it’s a bridge, but it’s a bridge with some massive gaps in it,” said Jason Gerstenberger, an independent agent who runs InsuredWithJason.com. “You need to understand that there could be a lot more limitations in the plan than you could ever imagine.”

Like any anti-poverty aid in the United States, this program for low- and no-income citizens has always had many restrictions, and under the Trump administration it has more, including new rules for 2027 that require most adults to work, volunteer or attend school for 80 hours per month.

To qualify at all in the 40 states (along with Washington, D.C.) that expanded Medicaid access under the A.C.A., your income level can’t be more than 138 percent of the federal poverty level, which is a total adjusted household income of $22,025 for a single person; $45,540 for a family of four. In Hawaii and Alaska, the income numbers are higher.

In the other 10 states, such as Mississippi, adults won’t qualify if they aren’t disabled, caring for minor children or meet other special rules.

Because Medicaid eligibility and rules are complex and can vary widely from state to state, it’s best to check with your individual state Medicaid office. You can find some details and contact information at Medicaid.gov.

People who are members of or can join a small business, trade or professional association may be able to get group insurance through the association. One example is the Small Business Service Bureau, which helps small businesses looking to find affordable coverage for businesses, individuals and families. These plans also come with their own caps, limits and fine print, so shop carefully.

“The problem is, people are left with sort of a dizzying array of choices along a lot of different dimensions,” said Mr. Weil of AARP. “They really need to move carefully.”

item.title: How to Make More Cars in America? Rivian’s C.E.O. Has Some Ideas.
item.description:
Building a car company from “zero is pretty hard,” RJ Scaringe likes to say. He founded Rivian, a buzzy electric vehicle start-up, in 2009 but delivering the firm’s first trucks and S.U.V.s would take a dozen years.

Developing the second model came easier than the first.

At every turn during a recent tour of Rivian’s sprawling seven-million-square-foot complex in Normal, Ill., a roughly two-hour drive south of Chicago, employees pointed out the ways that they streamlined the manufacturing process.

More than 400 robots in the body shop help with the early stages of assembly, such as welding together thick metal sheets. Rivian also built in-house tech systems that help workers communicate more efficiently.

The new S.U.V., the R2, was released in June to rave reviews. It starts at around $45,000, roughly half the cost of its predecessor, the R1.

Early excitement about the R2 is a rare bright spot for the electric vehicle industry in the United States. During President Trump’s second term, a tax credit for buying E.V.s was eliminated and fuel efficiency requirements for all new vehicles, a move expected to boost E.V. sales, were weakened.

In North America, sales of E.V.s fell 21 percent in the year through August, compared with the same period in 2025, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, a research firm. The largest U.S. automakers are backing away from E.V.s, and it would be even tougher for them if not for trade restrictions that have effectively banned cheaper Chinese E.V.s from the United States.

Mr. Scaringe, 43, is no stranger to the twists and turns in the industry. When he met with potential investors and suppliers in Rivian’s earliest days, it was shortly after G.M. and Chrysler had filed for bankruptcy. The investors were “audibly laughing” at him, he said.

Rivian, which is based in Irvine, Calif. and employs more than 15,000 people, expects to deliver up to 70,000 cars this year, a big jump from roughly 42,000 last year. That’s still a far cry from the 1.6 million cars that Tesla sold worldwide in 2025. And Rivian, which went public in 2021 and briefly had a market cap well over $100 billion, has yet to turn a profit.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

What did you learn from the rollout of the R1 model that helped inform the less expensive R2?

You see this in all types of consumer goods: You launch, you see the flagship come and then the more mass-market product follows.

R1 was always intended to be this flagship handshake with the world and then that would introduce the world to the brand.

Do you feel you should have come out with a more affordable model first?

No, I wouldn’t change it. You’re sourcing all these companies to make parts. Every part in the car that we don’t build ourselves, we have to get a supplier; and even the parts we build ourselves, we still have to get the raw materials.

We went into it knowing that we’re going to pay a 40 percent or 50 percent premium at the start of production to cover the risk of us being a new company.

As a result, it’s really hard for the first product to be an affordable one because you don’t have pricing leverage with suppliers. The hope, which took longer than we’d planned because of Covid and some of its supply challenges, was that after launch we’d be able to go back to suppliers and say: “The company’s now successful. We need to reduce pricing.”

Now, the C.E.O.s of those companies are flying to California or to Normal, Ill., to pitch their business.

The only thing I’d do differently — always you’d say this — is go faster on everything. But the order of events would have been the same.

In China, automakers bring a new vehicle to market in less than two years and sell it for half the price of a car in America. Chinese brands basically cannot sell here, but the question remains: How can the U.S. compete?

We should assume that in the fullness of time, China will likely be able to sell here.

It’s not like there’s some magic dust that China’s sprinkling. Their labor costs are much lower and their capital costs are much lower. In many cases, the capital costs are zero, or they have capital provided by the government. Other input costs, like electricity and utilities, are meaningfully lower than in the United States.

If we want to maintain an industrial footprint here in the United States, we have to have a way to bring equilibrium to these very different input cost structures. The way that’s largely done is through tariffs.

Say more about tariffs.

Every country has a choice: “Do we want to maintain that industry in our country?”

Cars is one that there are a lot of reasons we would want to keep that capability here. If tariffs go away, we have to be honest that a lot of manufacturing capacity is going to move to China. We’ve seen that before.

For all the things that we disagree on politically, I think, this is one where the right and the left agree: We need to do something to balance the difference in input costs between the United States and China.

There’s also an opportunity to use technology to bring equilibrium back. I started a company, Mind Robotics, last year. I’ve raised over a billion dollars for it to develop robotics that are capable of doing humanlike tasks.

Like humanoid robots?

More humanoid-ish. The robots have all the capabilities of a human but are not trying to directly replicate how a human looks.

Robots will work alongside humans in a line. The existence of A.I.-enabled robotics is what will allow us to take one of the biggest drivers of the difference in input costs, which are labor costs, and remove that.

There’s a lot of talk about trade policy these days. What does America need to do to make more cars here?

When we talk about trade as a society, we often simplify it and treat it like we’re buying and selling coffee cups in a very simple supply chain.

There are thousands of companies involved in making a Rivian. It’s impossible to say we’re going to make everything from the raw material mine through the vehicle in the United States. We don’t have everything. Sometimes materials are in places that don’t have governments that we are particularly friendly with or that follow policies that are similar to ours.

The distance between what’s easy to say politically and what has to happen practically is quite large. Policy needs to fill that gap.

The C.E.O. of your main competitor, Tesla, has a big profile. How do you want to be seen as a C.E.O.?

My personality is very different than Elon’s. He’s one of the most well-known people on the planet. I’m definitely not that. The brand and the products are going to speak for themselves.

When was the last time you talked to him?

We don’t. We’re not buds.

OK!

Not in a negative way.

Has consumer interest in E.V.s waned?

In the last few years, we’ve seen a shift from a policy point of view that’s not necessarily negative but also certainly not positive. It’s neutral at best. Some of the consumer-facing incentives have gone away. It’s not a bad thing in the sense that it’s an equal playing field, but the tailwind that was there disappeared.

Consumer sentiment surprisingly became somewhat political because of how electric vehicles are talked about. We’ve worked really hard to make sure that we don’t become political. We have a lot of Republican customers, a lot of Democrat customers.

How do you know?

We just ask people.

Are you thinking about making a car for an even lower price?

The next product, which we creatively call R3, is going to take the price point down. We haven’t announced pricing yet, but it will move materially lower. There’s a product beyond that, called R4, which again moves that further.

Tell me about your upbringing.

I’m from Florida. I grew up really into cars and into making things. Around 10, I realized I wanted to start a car company. I didn’t fully understand what that meant.

My dad’s a mechanical engineer. He has his own business, so I had the benefit of growing up around that. My mom’s a teacher — early childhood education.

Did your entrepreneurial father give you any helpful advice?

Not a specific piece of advice as much as it was his mind-set. He’s very risk tolerant. He was supportive of me starting Rivian in a way that most parents probably wouldn’t be.

It’s time for the lightning round. Don’t overthink it.

I probably will.

What’s the first car you owned?

A Volkswagen Corrado with a VR6.

What’s the last question you asked A.I.?

What is the percentage of the U.S. work force that works in agriculture? It’s a little less than 2 percent.

When you’re interviewing someone for a job, what is the most revealing question?

How someone has dealt with a challenging situation where there is no clear path or answer.

What is bad advice you hear given to young entrepreneurs?

Just going for blind optimism. Great entrepreneurs understand the need for optimism but also understand the challenges that have to be solved.

When will the last new gas-powered car be sold?

It will be a long time. But when do internal combustion vehicles drop below 1 percent market share? That’s a way to put it. In the United States, I’d say 2055.

item.title: China’s A.I. Makes a Great Leap Forward. But Its Economy Is Falling Behind.
item.description:
“The U.S. Lead Over China in AI Is All But Gone.”

“China Is AI-Maxxing.”

“China Just Erased America’s AI Lead.”

Those assessments of the artificial intelligence rivalry appeared in U.S. publications recently, and Xi Jinping will be pleased to have them in the air as he arrives in Washington this week for a state visit. Under Mr. Xi’s leadership, China has made huge strides in developing the most consequential technology of our times. What will be less discussed is that he is also the leader of an economy in its worst shape in decades.

The two facts are related.

Economists in China — even those closest to the state — have openly warned that the government is pouring too many resources into a technology that creates relatively few jobs, while doing too little to save the broader economy.

And it’s an economy in crisis: The country’s youth unemployment rate, excluding students, reached 18.9 percent in August. Consumers are not spending. During the first half of the year, domestic car sales fell markedly 20 percent from a year earlier, and housing sales fell another 14 percent, adding to years of decline. The country is in a deflationary spiral.

This summer, the economists’ warnings became a chorus. Li Daokui, a former adviser to the country’s central bank and a professor at Tsinghua University, said in July that China’s economy was “running too cold.” Its booming high-tech sectors, he said, could not lift the larger base.

Liu Shijin, another former adviser to the central bank, proposed at a forum in June to raise basic pension payouts, from $30 to $150 per month, for rural residents to shore up consumer demand.

At the same forum, Huang Haizhou, an adviser to the central bank, said Beijing must foster mild inflation and corporate profitability before sustained technological advancement could occur. “A country mired in deflation cannot achieve technological innovation,” he said.

The economists’ comments were earlier reported by Bloomberg and Chinese media.

The exact amount of government support for artificial intelligence is difficult to know. Stanford’s AI Index Report noted that state-initiated investment funds deployed an estimated $184 billion into A.I. firms from 2000 to 2023. Last year, Mr. Xi instructed the government to use every tool at its disposal, including tax breaks, government contracts, financing and access to infrastructure, to advance A.I. And, according to Bloomberg, China is preparing to spend around $295 billion over the next five years to build data centers across the country, which will be operated by state-owned firms.

The Chinese economists’ bluntness was itself revealing, as was the timing, just ahead of the regular midyear meeting of China’s ruling Politburo. They have been warned against sounding too pessimistic, and some have been censored or silenced for doing so. That these establishment figures were speaking so starkly right before the leadership was about to calibrate economic policy suggested how alarmed they had become.

Taken together, their message was clear: the Chinese economy was in trouble and an A.I.-centered allocation of resources could prove costly to ordinary people’s livelihoods and the country’s economic future.

The leadership gave their warnings little heed. When the Politburo meeting ended on July 30, the party acknowledged the need for “proactive” measures to boost the economy, but stuck with incremental stimulus policies and vowed to develop “an intelligent new economy.” State media reports broke with previous practice and did not announce a target for domestic growth.

Fixed-asset investment, including infrastructure, real estate and equipment, fell 4.1 percent in the first five months of the year. Mr. Li, the former central bank adviser, said a similar contraction happened only twice in the history of the People’s Republic: in 1961, at the height of the Great Famine, and in 1967, at the height of the Cultural Revolution. (It also fell in 1989 following the Tiananmen Square massacre, but it probably wouldn’t be wise to mention that at a meeting in Beijing.)

Mr. Xi has offered a revealing explanation of how he measures economic progress.

“We cannot look only at G.D.P. growth,” he said in a speech in March. What mattered, he argued, was China’s growing “hard power” and its development of advanced industries. In Mr. Xi’s view, slower growth does not necessarily signify failure if technological advancement proceeds “upward step by step.”

Rather than boosting household disposable income with cash or shopping vouchers or expanding the social safety net, as many economists have suggested, Mr. Xi believes that state-led technological rollouts will modernize traditional industries and unlock future economic value. But those gains could take years to materialize.

China cannot afford to sit out the A.I. race. And in the first half of 2026, investment in information services, a sector the National Bureau of Statistics said was being propelled by A.I., jumped 19.2 percent. The technology could transform its economy and strengthen its position in its competition against the United States.

But at what cost?

Xu Chenggang, a Chinese economist at Stanford, put plainly what his peers in Beijing could only imply. China has more fiscal and monetary flexibility than most countries because Beijing controls the banking system. Every yuan going into state-backed technology is a yuan not spent on employment and consumption.

“When you have only this much money, what do you spend it on?” he said.

In a crisis similar to what China is facing, many governments would use stimulus to create jobs, Mr. Xu said. When people have jobs, he said, they spend more, creating a positive economic feedback loop. Instead, Beijing is concentrating its investment in A.I., a technology that may exacerbate high unemployment by reducing demand for workers.

Some Chinese internet users are already calling the investment rush an “A.I. Great Leap Forward,” invoking Mao Zedong’s disastrous campaign of politically driven industrialization.

A.I. companies ultimately need more than government support. They need businesses and consumers willing and able to pay for their products, Mr. Xu said. By weakening household demand and business vitality, Beijing may be depriving its A.I. industry of the market it needs to become commercially successful.

China has repeatedly demonstrated that an authoritarian state can keep an unsustainable model operating longer than outsiders expect. But history also demonstrates that “longer” does not mean forever.

Sun Liping, a prominent sociologist in Beijing, invoked the Soviet Union. At its peak, its economy was roughly 70 percent the size of America’s, and it surpassed the United States in some fields of science and technology.

Yet its centrally managed economy eventually stalled.

China can produce vast quantities of increasingly sophisticated goods, Mr. Sun wrote in an article. But who in China will be able to afford them? Without buyers, products go unsold, businesses earn no profits, household incomes cannot rise and employment cannot improve.

“That,” he wrote, “is the fundamental problem with China’s economy today.”
